drills.q: Name the three caching layers in a production LLM stack and which one carries real correctness risk.
drills.a: Exact-match and prefix/prompt caching both require byte-identical matches (full request or shared prefix) and carry zero correctness risk. Semantic caching, matching by embedding similarity above a threshold, is the only layer that generalizes across paraphrasing -- and the only one that can be wrong on a hit.

drills.q: Is prompt/prefix caching the same thing as semantic caching?
drills.a: No. Prefix caching reuses the transformer's KV cache for a byte-identical shared prefix up to a cache breakpoint -- it does nothing for paraphrased queries and carries zero similarity-threshold risk, the opposite failure profile from semantic caching.

drills.q: Give a concrete example of a semantic-cache false hit and explain the mechanism.
drills.a: "Refund policy for annual plans" vs "...for monthly plans" can embed above 0.95 cosine similarity since they differ by one word, but the answers may be opposite. It happens because embedding closeness reflects overall topical/lexical similarity, not whether the one token that changes the answer was preserved.

drills.q: Why are static similarity thresholds fragile, and what does vCache do differently?
drills.a: A single global threshold assumes one cutoff fits every query cluster, but some tolerate loose matching safely while others (embedded dates/tiers/quantities) need tight matching. vCache learns a per-entry threshold online with a formal error-rate guarantee, reporting up to 12.5x higher hit rate and 26x lower error rate than static baselines at matched error budget.

drills.q: Walk through the cost arithmetic for a semantic cache at 40% hit rate, 1M queries/day, $0.003/query LLM cost, $0.0001/hit cost.
drills.a: Without cache: 1,000,000 x $0.003 = $3,000/day. With cache: 400,000 x $0.0001 + 600,000 x $0.003 = ~$1,840/day, a ~39% reduction that tracks the hit rate closely since the hit cost is near-negligible relative to a full LLM call.

drills.q: Why is a shared semantic cache across tenants dangerous, and what's the fix?
drills.a: If tenant A's query embeds close enough to a cached response built from tenant B's data, tenant A can receive an answer derived from tenant B's private content -- a real data leak, not just a wrong-answer bug. Fix: make tenant_id a hard filter in the cache lookup query itself, never a check applied after a candidate is retrieved.

drills.q: Design an invalidation strategy for a RAG semantic cache backed by a corpus that updates daily.
drills.a: Prefer event-driven invalidation: tag cache entries with the document/chunk IDs that fed their answer, and have the ingestion pipeline emit invalidation events for exactly the entries touched by an update. If per-entry tracking is too costly, fall back to versioned cache namespaces (reindex creates a fresh namespace) rather than TTL alone, which serves stale answers for the whole window and evicts unaffected entries too early.

drills.q: A stakeholder wants "as high a cache hit rate as possible." How do you respond?
drills.a: Hit rate isn't the objective alone -- pushing it up by loosening the threshold directly increases false-hit rate. Propose a target false-positive rate the business can tolerate, then tune hit rate as high as possible subject to that bound, ideally via an adaptive per-item method rather than a single guessed threshold.

drills.q: When is semantic caching actively the wrong choice? Give three categories.
drills.a: Personalized answers (same phrasing, different correct answer per user), time-sensitive information (stock prices, live inventory) where correctness decays faster than any safe TTL, and high-stakes domains (medical/legal/financial) where any residual false-hit rate has real consequences.

drills.q: Design the caching architecture for a multi-tenant, 22-locale RAG customer-support product where support policies vary by locale and change monthly.
drills.a: Layer all three caches, all keyed on tenant_id + locale. Exact-match and prefix caching run first with zero risk. Semantic caching is namespaced by (tenant_id, locale) as a hard filter in the lookup, never post-hoc, since both tenant leakage and cross-locale answer bleed are real risks. Use event-driven invalidation tied to the policy-ingestion pipeline, scoped per locale. Set similarity thresholds per locale (ideally adaptive) since paraphrase risk differs by language, and measure hit rate/positive-hit-rate per locale, not blended.
